transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, honestly, Doctor, it’s... it’s just that I don’t feel like myself anymore. Not for a good while now. I mean, I used to be able to just go about my day, you know? But lately, I barely talk to anyone. I just... I go completely flat. Quiet. Like all the air has been let out of a tire and there's just nothing left to keep it rolling. At work—I'm a janitor over at the community college, have been for years—I used to just grab my supplies and get to it. Now? Even just getting started on the cleaning route, just looking at the mop bucket, it feels like I'm trying to push a loaded cart uphill in the mud. I just stare at it and I can't seem to make my body move or care enough to make it move. And it's not just work, it's everything, but work is where I notice it most because I have to do it, you know? It's just this heavy, empty feeling, and I don't know where the old me went, but he's definitely not here right now.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Well, yes... actually, I have. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about it the other day, trying to figure out if I was just overtired or what. You know how it gets when you work the late shift, the building is mostly empty, and the acoustics in those old brick buildings can be strange. But this... this is different. It usually happens when I’m doing my rounds after hours. I’ll be down the C-wing—that's the one with the science labs, always smells a little like formaldehyde and floor wax—and I’ll be running the mop down the hall. Just me, the squeak of my shoes, and the mop hitting the baseboards. And then, clear as a bell, I’ll hear this man’s voice. Sometimes he just calls out my name, just real casual, like someone trying to get my attention. Other times, he’ll say something like, "You missed a spot right there," or "You're not doing it right." And Doctor, I swear to you, it sounds exactly like there is a full-grown man standing right by the stairwell, maybe ten feet away. Not an echo, not a whisper in my head, but a real person speaking right into the air. I always stop what I'm doing, my heart kind of jumps up into my throat, and I turn around ready to apologize or explain myself, but... there's never anyone there. Just the empty hallway and the emergency exit sign buzzing. I've even checked the stairwell, walked all the way up to the second floor just to be sure some student wasn't messing with me, but it's always completely empty. It really rattles me, to be honest. I just stand there holding the mop handle, feeling like I'm losing my grip on things, because how can you hear something so clearly when there's absolutely nothing there to make the sound?
Have you ever heard that voice during a time when you were not feeling depressed?

Well, you know, it's interesting you ask that, because I was trying to figure that out myself. You'd think, wouldn't you, that if it was just because I was feeling so low, it would go away when I had a good spell. And I did have a good spell, not too long ago actually. There was this stretch... oh, I'd say it lasted for several weeks, where that heavy, empty feeling kind of lifted some. Like the clouds parted just a little bit. I was actually getting through my meals again—I even started packing my own ham and cheese sandwiches for my shift instead of just staring at a piece of bread on the kitchen counter and giving up—and work was going a little better, too. I wasn't dreading the mop bucket quite as much, and the cart didn't feel like it weighed a thousand pounds. 

I thought, well, maybe I'm turning a corner here, maybe the old me is finally coming back. But the thing is, Doctor... the voice didn't stop. Even when I was feeling pretty decent, I'd be walking past that same stairwell in the C-wing, feeling perfectly fine, and clear as day, I'd still hear my name echoing out. Just right there in the air. And honestly, it almost made it more unsettling, because on top of hearing the voice when I wasn't even feeling depressed, I was still absolutely convinced that the hallway cameras were being used to track me. 

The college installed these little black dome cameras up in the corners of the ceilings a few years back, supposedly for security, you know, to watch the expensive lab equipment. But during those weeks, even when my mood was up and I was eating and working fine, I just knew whoever was on the other end of those cameras was watching my every single move. I felt like they were tracking where I went with the cleaning cart, documenting how long I spent in each hallway, maybe even using the system to mess with me. I'd stare up at the dark glass on those domes and just know they were zoomed right in on my face. So, yes, even when the depression took a backseat for a few weeks and I had some energy back, all of that... the voice in the stairwell, the cameras tracking me... it didn't go away at all. It was all still right there with me, every single night.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually high, euphoric, or full of energy?

Well, no, Doctor, I can't say that I have. You know, when you say "euphoric" or "full of energy," it almost sounds like something you'd see in a movie, somebody just bouncing off the walls or talking a mile a minute. I've seen some of the college kids acting like that during finals week, probably hopped up on those energy drinks they buy from the vending machines down in the student union—the ones in the bright neon cans that look like they're full of battery acid, you know? But for me? No, never. 

Even during that good stretch I was just telling you about, where I was packing my lunches and getting through my shift... that wasn't "high" energy. That was just... normal, I guess. Or what I remember normal feeling like. It was just enough energy to push the mop and not feel like I was dragging a ball and chain behind me. But I've never had a time where I felt, like, on top of the world or buzzing with electricity or anything like that. 

My whole life, really, I've been a pretty steady, quiet guy, maybe a bit on the slower side when it comes to getting worked up about things. Even back when I was in my twenties, taking a few classes at the community college myself before I eventually just started working there full-time, I was never the type to pull all-nighters or get overly excited about much of anything. I just plodded along. So, no, nothing like that. It's usually just that heavy, empty feeling I told you about, or, if I'm really lucky, just regular old tired at the end of a shift. Never euphoric. Honestly, I don't think my brain even knows how to do that.
Have the voice and the feeling that the cameras are tracking you been going on for at least 6 months?

Six months? Oh, well... actually, it's been quite a bit longer than that. If I sit and really trace it back—and I do, I spend a lot of time trying to make sense of all this when I'm just pushing the mop around—it’s been... gosh, it’s been about 11 months now. 

I can pinpoint it pretty exactly, too, because... well, you know how colleges operate, they have their cycles. It was right around the time we were doing the big deep clean getting ready for the summer sessions last year. I remember because my supervisor had me stripping all the old wax off the floors in the main administration building. That’s a miserable job, by the way. The chemical stripper they make us use smells absolutely awful, way worse than the formaldehyde over in the science wing, and you have to let it sit on the linoleum until it turns into this thick, slippery slurry before you can even scrape it up. 

Anyway, I was working on that, just sweating through my uniform, and I happened to look up, and that was the very first time I really understood that the cameras were tracking me. I saw the little red light blink on the dome, and the lens just... shifted, right at me. I could feel it zooming in. And then, it couldn't have been more than a week after that when I first heard the man's voice calling my name by the stairwell in the C-wing. 

So, yes, the voices and all those worries about being watched, it's been going on for about 11 months now. And let me tell you, Doctor, 11 months is a very, very long time to live like this. Day in, day out. You go to work, you punch your card, you load up your cart with paper towels and glass cleaner, and the whole time you're just waiting for it. Waiting for the voice to tell you you missed a spot, waiting for the camera dome to pivot and follow you down the hall. It wears you down to the bone, it really does. I mean, nearly a whole year of looking over your shoulder... sometimes I wonder how I've even managed to keep showing up every night. But what else are you going to do, you know? You have to pay the bills, you have to keep your job. But yeah... eleven months. It's been a long eleven months.
Have there been at least 2 weeks when you were hearing the voice or felt the cameras were tracking you while your mood felt normal, without depression?

Well, yes, Doctor, like I was trying to explain just a little bit ago... there was exactly that kind of stretch. Remember I was telling you about packing my own ham and cheese sandwiches again instead of just staring at the bread? That lasted for several weeks, actually. My mood had definitely lifted some during that time. I wasn't waking up with that terrible, crushing weight on my chest, and I was actually getting through my meals and my shifts at work a little better. I wasn't dreading the mop bucket nearly as much, and I didn't have that dark, heavy depression dragging me down. 

But, just like I said, even during those several weeks when I felt pretty normal—or at least, my version of normal—I still heard my name echoing in that C-wing stairwell. Clear as a bell, just hanging right there in the air. And I stayed absolutely convinced that those little black dome cameras in the hallways were being used to track me. It didn't stop at all. You'd think catching a break from the sadness would mean catching a break from the rest of it, wouldn't you? But no. I’d be walking down the hall, feeling perfectly fine, maybe even humming a little tune to myself because the shift was going well, and I'd look up at that dark glass on the ceiling and just know they were watching my cart, documenting my every single step. So, yes, definitely at least two weeks. Several weeks, really, where the depression took a backseat, but the voice and the cameras were right there with me the whole entire time.
